newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN LABOR REPUDIATES HANSON'S PARTY.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN LABOR REPUDIATES HANSON'S PARTY.

text.p: The Australian Labor Opposition took a stand against populist politician Pauline Hanson on Friday, declaring it would urge voters to give her One Nation Party the lowest priority at the next election.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley challenged Liberal-National Prime Minister John Howard to match Labor's policy.

"By this action today (Labor) has made clear its complete repudiation of the racist views of Pauline Hanson and the One Nation Party, and has committed itself to a firm stand against bigotry at the next federal election," he said.

Party directions to voters are crucial under Australia's preferential voting system, which seeks to produce consensus members of parliament by distributing votes according to the electors' numbered preferences.

Members of the two big blocs win almost all the lower house seats but if the contest is tight it will be determined by redistributed votes from minor candidates, who are progressively eliminated until someone has more than 50 percent support.
Two parties might agree to each urge its supporters to give their second-preference votes to the other.
Hanson, elected last year, has won about 10 percent voter support with her opposition to Aboriginal welfare, economic reform and immigration, especially Asian immigration.
The major parties reject Hanson's views but Howard's administration has been careful not to alienate her supporters.

"It is not too late for the prime minister to join the opposition in our efforts to ensure no comfort is given to, nor any political benefit sought from, those who peddle racist and bigoted views," Beazley said.
Hanson first stirred debate when she made her maiden speech, especially since some of Australia's more vocal radio presenters endorsed her claims.
But Howard said little to rebut her views. His opponents said he was scared that she had too much support for him to say anything.
Howard himself said that as prime minister he should not have to respond to the every statement by a minor independent member of parliament.
